name: St Brice's Day massacre

location.note: Æthelred II ordered the killing of Danes across England; Oxford, where Danes were burned in St Frideswide's church, is the only well-documented location.

narrative: Æthelred II ordered the killing of 'all the Danish men who were in England'. A royal charter of 1004 records that Danes in Oxford fled into St Frideswide's church, which was burned.
outcome: Numbers killed are unknown. Later tradition linked the massacre to Swein Forkbeard's invasions.
disagreements: How widely the order was carried out is debated; it probably affected recent Danish arrivals rather than the settled population of the Danelaw.

name: Siege of Durham
narrative: Malcolm II of Alba besieged Durham and was defeated by a relieving force under Uhtred, son of the earl of Bamburgh.
outcome: Scottish defeat; Uhtred was rewarded with the earldom of Northumbria.
disagreements: Known mainly from the later tract De obsessione Dunelmi; the date is not certain.

name: Battle of Ringmere
narrative: A Danish army landed at Ipswich and defeated the East Anglian force at Ringmere; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names several English leaders killed.
outcome: Danish victory; the Danes ravaged East Anglia for three months.

name: Siege of Canterbury
narrative: The Danish army besieged and took Canterbury through treachery, capturing Archbishop Ælfheah, who was killed at Greenwich in April 1012.
outcome: City captured and sacked.

name: Swein Forkbeard's conquest of England

location.note: Mapped at Swein's landing on the Trent; the campaign covered much of England.

narrative: Swein landed at Gainsborough, received the submission of the Danelaw, and moved south. London submitted and Æthelred fled to Normandy.
outcome: Swein accepted as king late in 1013; he died in February 1014.

name: Cnut's war for England

location.note: War-level record; see the linked battles.

participants: auth-england:Kingdom of England (Æthelred II, Edmund Ironside)
narrative: Cnut invaded in 1015. After Æthelred's death in April 1016 his son Edmund Ironside fought five battles against Cnut.
outcome: After Assandun the kingdom was divided; Edmund died on 30 November 1016 and Cnut became king of all England.

name: Siege of London
narrative: Cnut's fleet besieged London, reportedly dragging ships around the bridge, but the city held.
outcome: Siege abandoned.

name: Battle of Penselwood
narrative: First of Edmund Ironside's battles against Cnut.
outcome: Indecisive; recorded as an English success in some accounts.

name: Battle of Sherston
narrative: A two-day battle fought soon after midsummer 1016.
outcome: Indecisive.
disagreements: Identification of the Chronicle's 'Sceorstan' with Sherston is traditional but not certain.

name: Battle of Otford
narrative: Edmund defeated the Danes at Otford and pursued them into Sheppey.
outcome: English victory.

name: Battle of Assandun

location.note: The site of 'Assandun' is disputed between Ashingdon and Ashdon.

narrative: Cnut defeated Edmund after Eadric Streona's contingent abandoned the field. The Chronicle lists many English nobles killed, including Ealdorman Ulfcytel and Bishop Eadnoth.
outcome: Decisive Danish victory; partition of the kingdom at Alney, then Cnut's sole rule.
disagreements: Location disputed between Ashingdon and Ashdon.

name: Battle of Carham

date.note: Usually dated 1018; some scholars argue for 1016.

narrative: Malcolm II, with Owain of Strathclyde, defeated the Northumbrians at Carham on the Tweed.
outcome: Scottish victory, traditionally seen as securing Lothian for the Scottish kings.
disagreements: Date (1016 or 1018), the identity of the Northumbrian leader, and how decisive the battle was for Lothian are all debated.

name: Battle of Rhyd-y-groes

location.placeName: Ford on the Severn near Forden

narrative: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn defeated a Mercian army at a ford on the Severn; Edwin, brother of Earl Leofric, was killed.
outcome: Welsh victory.

name: Battle of the Seven Sleepers (Dunsinane)

location.note: The battle site is not recorded; Dunsinane is a later tradition.

narrative: Earl Siward of Northumbria invaded Scotland by land and sea and defeated Macbeth on the day of the Seven Sleepers. Siward's son Osbeorn was among the dead.
outcome: Northumbrian victory; Macbeth remained king until 1057.

name: Sack of Hereford
narrative: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn and the exiled Ælfgar routed Earl Ralph's force and sacked Hereford, burning the cathedral.
outcome: Welsh victory; Harold Godwinson refortified Hereford.

name: Battle of Lumphanan
narrative: Macbeth was killed by the forces of Malcolm, son of Duncan I.
outcome: Death of Macbeth; Malcolm III became king in 1058 after the death of Lulach.

name: Harold's campaign in Wales
narrative: Harold and Tostig attacked Wales by land and sea. Gruffydd ap Llywelyn, ruler of all Wales, was killed by his own men in August 1063.
outcome: Collapse of Gruffydd's unified Welsh rule.

name: Battle of Fulford
participants: auth-england:Northumbrian and Mercian levies (Edwin and Morcar)
narrative: Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls outside York.
outcome: Norwegian victory; York submitted.

name: The invasions of 1066

location.note: Campaign-level record; see linked battles and William's documented itinerary.

narrative: Two invasions within weeks: Harald Hardrada in the north, then William of Normandy in the south.
outcome: William crowned at Westminster on 25 December 1066.

name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
narrative: After a rapid march north, Harold surprised the Norwegian army at Stamford Bridge. Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed.
outcome: Decisive English victory; the Chronicle says the survivors needed only 24 of their ships to return.

name: William of Normandy's campaign, 1066
narrative: William landed at Pevensey, fortified Hastings, won the battle near Hastings, secured Dover and Canterbury, burned Southwark, crossed the Thames at Wallingford and received the submission of the English leaders at Berkhamsted.
outcome: Coronation of William I at Westminster, 25 December 1066.

name: Battle of Hastings
narrative: An all-day battle on the ridge later occupied by Battle Abbey. Harold and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were killed.
outcome: Decisive Norman victory, leading to the Norman conquest of England.
disagreements: Alternative sites (e.g. Caldbec Hill, Crowhurst) have been proposed, but the abbey site remains the registered battlefield.

name: Siege of Exeter
narrative: Exeter resisted William I for 18 days before negotiating a surrender; a castle was then built in the city.
outcome: Surrender on terms; Rougemont Castle founded.

name: Capture of York
narrative: A Danish fleet joined northern English rebels. The two Norman castles at York were stormed and burned and much of the garrison killed.
outcome: Rebel victory, provoking William's Harrying of the North.

name: Harrying of the North

location.note: Devastation across a wide region; shown as a broad area.

narrative: William I's forces systematically destroyed crops, livestock and settlements across the north in the winter of 1069–70. Famine followed.
outcome: Long-term depopulation; Domesday Book (1086) records many Yorkshire vills as 'waste'.
disagreements: Orderic Vitalis wrote that more than 100,000 died; modern historians regard the figure as unverifiable. The extent of 'waste' in Domesday is also debated.

name: Siege of Ely
narrative: English rebels held the Isle of Ely in the fens; William built a causeway and the defenders submitted.
outcome: Royal victory; Morcar imprisoned, Hereward escaped.

name: Siege of Norwich Castle
participants: Rebels of Earl Ralph de Gael (Revolt of the Earls)
narrative: During the Revolt of the Earls, Ralph de Gael's wife Emma held Norwich castle against a royal siege for about three months.
outcome: Surrender on terms; the defenders went into exile.

name: Battle of Mynydd Carn
participants: auth-welsh:Gruffudd ap Cynan and Rhys ap Tewdwr
narrative: Gruffudd ap Cynan and Rhys ap Tewdwr defeated and killed Trahaearn ap Caradog, a turning point in the struggle for Gwynedd and Deheubarth.
outcome: Victory for Gruffudd and Rhys.
disagreements: The site has never been securely identified.

name: Rebellion of 1088
participants: Rebel barons supporting Robert Curthose (Odo of Bayeux)
narrative: Barons led by Odo of Bayeux rose in favour of Robert Curthose against William II.
outcome: Royal victory; Odo exiled.

name: Siege of Pevensey
narrative: William II besieged Odo in Pevensey for about six weeks until hunger forced surrender.
outcome: Royal victory.

name: Siege of Rochester
participants: Rebel garrison (Odo of Bayeux, Eustace of Boulogne)
narrative: The rebel garrison at Rochester was blockaded by siege castles and surrendered.
outcome: Royal victory.

name: William II takes Carlisle
narrative: William II drove out Dolfin, built a castle at Carlisle and settled the district with southern English peasants.
outcome: Carlisle and the surrounding district brought under the English crown.

name: Battle of Alnwick (1093)
narrative: Malcolm III and his eldest son Edward were killed in an ambush by Robert de Mowbray's men while raiding Northumberland.
outcome: Death of Malcolm III; succession crisis in Scotland.

name: Welsh revolt of 1094
participants: auth-welsh:Welsh rulers (Gruffudd ap Cynan, Cadwgan ap Bleddyn)
narrative: A general Welsh rising destroyed many recently built Norman castles in north and west Wales.
outcome: Norman control in Gwynedd largely ended; Pembroke held out.

name: Siege of Bamburgh
participants: Robert de Mowbray, earl of Northumbria
narrative: William II besieged the rebel earl Robert de Mowbray's stronghold, building a siege castle ('Malvoisin').
outcome: Mowbray captured; his wife surrendered the castle under threat of his blinding.

name: The Anarchy (civil war of Stephen and Matilda)

location.note: War-level record; see linked battles and sieges.

participants: Empress Matilda and Robert of Gloucester
narrative: Succession war between Stephen and Henry I's daughter Matilda, with Scottish intervention in the north.
outcome: Treaty of Winchester/Wallingford (1153): Matilda's son Henry recognised as heir.

name: Siege of Exeter Castle
narrative: Stephen besieged Baldwin de Redvers in Exeter castle for about three months; the garrison surrendered when its wells failed.
outcome: Royal victory.

name: Battle of Crug Mawr
narrative: The sons of Gruffudd ap Cynan routed the Anglo-Norman forces near Cardigan; many fugitives drowned in the Teifi.
outcome: Welsh victory; Ceredigion recovered from Norman control.

name: Battle of Clitheroe
narrative: A Scottish raiding army under William fitz Duncan defeated an English force near Clitheroe.
outcome: Scottish victory.

name: Siege of Wark
narrative: David I's forces besieged Wark castle at intervals through 1138; the starving garrison surrendered in November.
outcome: Castle surrendered and was destroyed.

name: Battle of the Standard
participants: auth-england:Northern English barons and levies (Archbishop Thurstan)
narrative: An English army gathered by Archbishop Thurstan around a cart bearing church banners defeated David I's invading army.
outcome: English victory; but David retained much of Cumberland and Northumberland by the Treaty of Durham (1139).
disagreements: Chroniclers such as Richard of Hexham give very large Scottish losses (about 10,000) that are generally considered exaggerated; no figure is used here.

name: First Battle of Lincoln
participants: Angevin forces (Robert of Gloucester, Ranulf of Chester)
narrative: Stephen, besieging Lincoln castle, was attacked by a relief army and captured after fighting on foot.
outcome: Stephen captured; Matilda briefly in the ascendant.

name: Rout of Winchester
participants: Royalist forces (Queen Matilda, William of Ypres)
Angevin forces (Empress Matilda, Robert of Gloucester)
narrative: The Empress's forces besieging Bishop Henry's palace were themselves encircled; in the retreat Robert of Gloucester was captured.
outcome: Royalist victory; Robert exchanged for Stephen.

name: Siege of Oxford
narrative: Stephen besieged the Empress in Oxford castle for about three months; she escaped across the frozen countryside in December.
outcome: Castle surrendered after Matilda's escape.

name: Battle of Wilton
narrative: Robert of Gloucester attacked Stephen's force at Wilton; the king narrowly escaped.
outcome: Angevin victory.
